overview.title: Event overview
overview.content: On the evening of 24 June 2026, at around 18:04 local time (2204/2205 UTC), two major earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela about 39-40 seconds apart: a magnitude 7.2 foreshock near San Felipe, Yaracuy (depth about 22 km) and a magnitude 7.5 mainshock near Yumare, Veroes, Yaracuy (depth about 10 km, shallow), with epicentres also described as some 28-30 km north-west of Montalbán, Carabobo, and west of Caracas near Yaracuy and Carabobo (OCHA, PAHO/WHO). USGS recorded this as the strongest earthquake in Venezuela in more than 125 years, generating very strong to violent shaking (peak intensity approaching MMI 9) felt across a densely populated corridor including Caracas, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, Falcón and Yaracuy, and as far as Colombia (Data Friendly Space/USGS/Al Jazeera). The shocks occurred on the Boconó-Morón-El Pilar fault system at the Caribbean-South American plate boundary; USGS issued a Red PAGER alert indicating high probable casualties and extensive damage, and a brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was cancelled within about an hour.

hazards.title: Hazard and cascading hazards
hazards.content: The primary hazard was the dual shallow earthquake sequence (M7.2 and M7.5), followed by extensive aftershock activity: at least 20 aftershocks within two hours of the mainshock (six felt in Caracas), more than 302 aftershocks by 26 June (OCHA), nearly 1,000 by 6 July (UNFPA), and over 1,000 by mid-July, including a M5.1 event near Tucacas (Falcón) on 25 June and a M4.4 aftershock near Guatire (Miranda) on 26 June; USGS estimated about a 40% chance of a magnitude 6+ aftershock in the first week. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR flagged secondary hazard risk from the onset of the annual rainy season, with potential for heavy rains, hurricanes or tropical low-pressure systems triggering landslides and mud flows in already seismically weakened slopes, requiring landslide and debris-flow mapping in the North Coastal Range. PAHO also identified elevated risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, polio), acute diarrheal disease, cholera, and other water/vector-borne illnesses linked to displacement, overcrowding and damaged WASH systems.

exposure_vulnerability.title: Exposure and vulnerability
exposure_vulnerability.content: UNDP's RAPIDA assessment estimated 8.6 million people exposed to above-moderate shaking across northern Venezuela, including about 2.1 million exposed to stronger shaking, with 1.7 million structures located in affected areas. The earthquake struck a context of protracted economic and humanitarian crisis: Venezuela ranked 24th of 97 crises on the INFORM Severity Index (high severity, 7.6/10) as of May 2026, with nearly 8 million people already in humanitarian need before the quakes (IRC/UNDRR). ACAPS and REACH note widespread pre-existing vulnerabilities in the hardest-hit states (La Guaira, Caracas, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, Falcón): weak shelter, water and health systems, substandard and unreinforced construction with poor enforcement of building codes, informal settlements on unstable hillsides, a 94% poverty rate and 46% multidimensional poverty rate in La Guaira, 62% of housing in fragile condition with repair needs, and a Protection Cluster that had reached only 8% of its 1.9 million target population by April 2026. About 30% of the population is under 18 and 9% over 65 (IFRC), and years of emigration (roughly 8 million people) left critical workforce gaps affecting search-and-rescue and recovery capacity (IRC).

impacts.title: Impacts
impacts.content: Casualty figures rose steadily and sometimes diverged between sources: Data Friendly Space reported 164 dead/971 injured on 25 June (up from an initial 32 dead); OCHA Sitrep No.3 (26 June) reported a provisional 920 dead/3,360 injured and REACH the same day cited 589 dead/2,980 injured; by 29 June MSF reported 1,430 dead/3,230 injured while UNHCR cited 1,719 dead, 5,034 hospitalised and 15,866 affected; IFRC's 1 July brief noted "tens of thousands" reported missing, with USGS modelling giving even odds that final deaths fall between 1,000-10,000 and a 30% chance of exceeding 10,000; UNFPA (6 July) reported 3,342 dead/16,470 injured, rising to 4,490 dead by UNICEF's 15 July count and 5,208 dead per CESVI by 20 July, with people injured holding at 16,740 across PAHO, UNFPA and CESVI reports from early July onward. Displacement estimates also varied: OCHA cited over 3,000 displaced (26 June), UNHCR 15,000+ affected/displaced by 29 June, UNFPA 17,345 who lost homes and 10,702 in 79 temporary camps by 6 July, rising to 17,907 homeless per UNICEF (15 July) and CESVI (20 July). Infrastructure damage reports progressed from 1,423 affected structures (OCHA, 26 June) to 2,501 damaged sites including 774 housing units, 189 fully collapsed, and 38 hospitals (UNHCR, 29 June), with CESVI (20 July) citing 856 affected buildings; UNDP estimated preliminary direct physical damage at US$6.7 billion (about 6% of GDP) within hours of the quake, while UNDRR's 3 July analytical estimate put total direct damage at approximately US$37 billion (US$24 billion to buildings, US$13 billion to infrastructure), equivalent to roughly 3-4% of exposed stock. Key infrastructure losses included closure of Maiquetía/Simón Bolívar International Airport, suspension of Caracas Metro and railways, multi-state power outages, and damage to electricity, water, telecommunications, roads and bridges.

prevention.title: Prevention and mitigation
prevention.content: Documents report significant prevention gaps rather than successful mitigation measures: ACAPS states that most buildings in Venezuela are unlikely to have been built in line with modern earthquake regulations, citing reports of a lack of enforcement of building standards (CNN, APnews). IFRC and ACAPS both note widespread informal settlements built on unstable hillsides and vulnerable unreinforced construction as pre-existing risk factors that amplified damage. No risk-financing, retrofitting programmes, or land-use planning measures prior to the event are described in the documents.

preparedness.title: Preparedness
preparedness.content: The documents do not describe specific pre-event early warning systems, contingency plans, drills or stockpiles for this earthquake; FUNVISIS (Venezuela's seismological institute) is referenced only as an information source, not for prior monitoring performance. A brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was issued by relevant authorities and cancelled within about an hour, indicating some monitoring capacity was operational at the time of the event (Data Friendly Space, citing USGS/CNN/NPR). Pre-existing weak institutional capacity is implied by ACAPS' observation that censorship and limited transparency have historically weakened public trust in official information, likely hindering situational awareness and risk communication during the response.

response.title: Response
response.content: The Venezuelan government declared a national state of emergency and designated La Guaira a disaster zone; Acting President Delcy Rodríguez and National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez provided official casualty updates from 25-26 June. The Venezuelan Red Cross began search-and-rescue in the Capital District on 24 June and received CHF 2 million from IFRC's DREF on 25 June; IFRC launched a CHF 50 million Emergency Appeal on 26 June (later CHF 55 million Federation-wide) targeting 300,000 people, and set up a field hospital at Jorge García Carmeiro Stadium plus a Field Operations Centre. International UNDAC and USAR teams under INSARAG coordination arrived from 25 June; authorities imposed temporary access restrictions to La Guaira state from the night of 26 June to prioritize search and rescue. The Expanded Health Cluster, co-led with the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS), was activated 26 June to consolidate a single response mechanism integrating state actors, UN agencies and NGOs. UN agencies scaled up: UNICEF, UNFPA (targeting 64,000-230,000 people for SRH/GBV services), UNHCR (seeking $14.8-14.85 million for 30,000 people), WFP-supported logistics, and PAHO/WHO delivered medical supplies and equipment, including to Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere by mid-August. NGOs including MSF, Good Neighbors, CESVI, Project HOPE/Proyecto Esperanza and the Turkish Red Crescent mobilized emergency relief, health posts and needs assessments. Constraints included blocked roads from debris, damaged Maiquetía airport, disrupted telecommunications, erratic fuel availability, and logistics congestion at the airport and Port of La Guaira, as flagged by UNICEF and the OCHA Logistics Working Group ($0.8M requirement).

recovery.title: Recovery and reconstruction
recovery.content: By late July, CESVI reported the response transitioning from immediate emergency to a more structured, large-scale operation, and by 12 August (PAHO Sitrep No.9, seven weeks on) efforts were shifting toward early recovery, including rehabilitation planning at priority health facilities, restoration of intensive care and maternity capacity at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, and a USD 18 million PAHO Revolving Fund credit line to support national vaccine supply security. OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July 2026) and UNICEF's HAC Appeal Addendum ($65.7 million to reach 470,000 people, including 167,000 children) outline sector plans aligned with the earthquake addendum targeting 1.3 million affected people across 7 states. IRC warned on 22 July that without urgent investment in local economies and livelihoods, Venezuela risked spiraling into a deeper crisis, citing UNDRR's $37 billion damage estimate and noting that over half the population already lived in extreme poverty before the quakes.

needs_gaps.title: Needs and gaps
needs_gaps.content: The Health Cluster (27 June) identified critical gaps in food, safe water, hygiene kits, non-food items, clothing and safe temporary shelter, alongside needs for logistics support, specialized medical personnel, mental health/psychosocial support, and protection pathways for unaccompanied children. REACH highlighted pre-existing weak shelter, WASH and health systems in Aragua, La Guaira, Carabobo and Falcón limiting absorptive capacity, with water cited as the top priority need nationally since March 2026. Project HOPE's assessment (16 health facilities, 48 hours post-event; expanded to 12 facilities/160 households) found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure and protection mechanisms. UNFPA flagged unmet needs in survivor-centred GBV and SRH services amid overcrowded shelters and family separation. PAHO (10 July) noted persistent gaps in registration and follow-up of injured and hospitalized patients, likely causing underestimation of casualties, plus a severely strained health system with shortages of personnel, medicines, supplies and surgical capacity even before the quakes.

lessons.title: Lessons and recommendations
lessons.content: ACAPS noted that censorship, limited transparency and restrictions on media and civil society have weakened public trust in official information, increasing reliance on informal networks and complicating coordination between authorities, responders and communities, delaying assistance delivery and targeting. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR Environmental Quick Note recommended guiding the response with Sphere Shelter Standard 7 and ECHO Minimum Environmental Requirements, including environmental impact assessment, sustainable materials, debris reuse/recycling, safe solid waste management and protection of ecological value at temporary settlement sites, alongside daily monitoring of rainfall/landslide risk. IRC stressed that immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support is critical in the early recovery window to prevent the disaster from deepening the pre-existing humanitarian crisis, given the workforce gaps created by prior mass emigration.

confidence.title: Information quality
confidence.content: Reporting is frequent and multi-sourced (OCHA, PAHO/WHO, UNDP, UNHCR, UNICEF, UNFPA, IFRC, ACAPS, REACH, UNDRR, NGOs) spanning day +0 to +48, allowing a fairly detailed timeline, but casualty and damage figures are explicitly described by multiple agencies as preliminary and subject to change, with notable discrepancies between sources reporting on the same or similar dates (e.g., 589 vs 920 dead on 26 June; 1,423 vs 2,501 vs 1,500 vs 856 damaged structures across different sitreps). Figures for missing persons remain ambiguous and unreconciled (IFRC), and later UNICEF/CESVI death tolls (4,490-5,208 by mid-to-late July) are not cross-confirmed by PAHO, which continued citing the 3,342-3,300+ figure as of 10 July. No information is provided on pre-event early warning system performance, detailed prevention/building-code history, or final reconstruction costs, leaving medium-to-low confidence in those areas despite high confidence in response and impact chronology.

passages.text: Date: 26 June 2026 Good Neighbors Statement on the Venezuela Earthquake Good Neighbors expresses its deepest sympathy to the communities affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026. The earthquakes caused widespread destruction to homes, public infrastructure, and essential services, leaving thousands of families in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. Families have lost loved ones, their homes, and their sense of safety. Children, in particular, are facing fear, uncertainty, and significant disruption to their daily lives. As aftershocks continue, many families remain displaced, taking shelter in cars, makeshift tents, and other temporary accommodations without reliable access to electricity, safe drinking water, food, or protection services. In response to this crisis, Good Neighbors is preparing an emergency response to protect the safety, well-being, and dignity of children and their families. Initial support is expected to include emergency shelter and other essential relief items, while additional assistance will be determined based on ongoing needs assessments and operational feasibility.

Maiquetía International Airport closed without commercial flights; Caracas Metro and railways suspended; power outages in multiple states. International teams are already present in the country, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams under INSARAG coordination. **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following the two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) of 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre off the coast some 28–30 km north-west of Montalbán (Carabobo). Authorities report more than 302 aftershocks, including a magnitude 5.1 event reported in Tucacas (Falcón state) on the night of 25 June, and a magnitude 4.4 aftershock northeast of Guatire (Miranda state) in the early hours of 26 June, sustaining high-risk conditions.

passages.title: Venezuela faces US$6.7 billion in economic losses from earthquakes, UNDP estimates
passages.text: **Caracas/New York, 26 June 2026** – The earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June caused significant human suffering and loss of life, while also severely affecting livelihoods, infrastructure, and essential services. This includes a preliminary estimate of $6.7 billion in direct physical damage, equivalent to around 6% of GDP, according to a satellite-based Rapid Digital Assessment (RAPIDA) by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). While the economic impact is substantial, the greatest loss is borne by the people and communities. The assessment is based on seismic modelling, satellite imagery and population data and was carried out in the hours after the quake. The quakes, measuring magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, hit near Venezuela’s northern coast and were felt across major population and economically important areas, including Caracas and the states of La Guaira, Carabobo, Miranda, Yaracuy, and Aragua. UNDP estimates that 1.7 million structures were in affected areas, including large numbers in the hardest-hit states. The analysis found that around 8.6 million people were exposed to above moderate shaking across the country’s north, including around 2.1 million exposed to stronger shaking.

passages.title: Venezuela June 2026 Earthquake: Emergency Situation Overview (26/06/2026)
passages.text: The earthquake struck areas where essential services were already operating under severe strain, limiting their capacity to absorb additional shocks. Across several affected states, HSM data indicated widespread housing deterioration, serious water access problems, and health systems facing shortages of medicines, equipment and trained staff. These pre-existing constraints are likely to amplify humanitarian needs as displacement and demand for services increase. The earthquake risks disrupting fragile livelihoods and reversing recent improvements in household food access. As food insecurity in Venezuela is primarily driven by limited purchasing power rather than market availability, households relying on daily labour, small businesses or informal income may see their ability to meet basic needs deteriorate rapidly, particularly where alternative coping mechanisms such as remittances or social assistance are limited. Pre-existing vulnerabilities suggest that humanitarian needs may be particularly severe in specific affected states rather than evenly distributed. HSM data indicate that Aragua, La Guaira, Carabobo and Falcón consistently reported some of the weakest pre-earthquake conditions across shelter, water access and health services, suggesting these areas may face greater challenges absorbing the impacts of the earthquake. CONTEXT & RATIONALE On 24 June 2026 at around 18:04 local time, two powerful earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) struck northern Venezuela seconds apart. Both were shallow with the main shock’s depth of around 10 km. The fault runs east towards one of the country’s most densely populated corridors, home to Caracas and several major coastal cities. Significant damage was reported in Caracas and the states of La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, Falcón, and Yaracuy.

passages.text: **CONTEXT** The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (hereinafter “Venezuela”) entered 2026 with pre-existing socioeconomic and humanitarian vulnerabilities that continue to affect population health and the resilience of essential services. Although some macroeconomic indicators showed modest improvement in recent years, millions of people continue to face difficulties accessing health care, safe water, food, and other basic services. These underlying conditions have increased the country's vulnerability to the health impacts of emergencies and disasters. On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck northern Venezuela within less than one minute of each other, with epicentres located west of Caracas near the states of Yaracuy andCarabobo. The earthquakes generated very strong to violent ground shaking across a densely populated corridor, causing widespread damage to homes, health facilities, transport infrastructure, and essential services. As of 5 July 2026, official reports indicate more than 3,300 deaths, over 16,700 injuries, approximately 17,300 people displaced after losing their homes, and more than 6,400 people rescued. Three health facilities have been reported as damaged, while damage assessments continue in the affected areas. Numerous aftershocks followed the main event, further complicating emergency response and recovery efforts. This document provides a comprehensive assessment of the public health situation in Venezuela following the earthquakes of June 2026. It covers the context of the emergency, the impact on the population and health services, and an analysis of key health risks and priority actions for the humanitarian response.

passages.text: On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela, adding a new layer of humanitarian needs to an already fragile context. Two weeks after the earthquakes, official figures reported 4,490 deaths, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people left without housing. The earthquakes have created a major child-focused humanitarian emergency on top of already significant needs. Children and families have lost homes, schools, access to safe water, health services, and protection systems, while aftershocks continue to heighten risks and complicate recovery. UNICEF requires **US$65.7 million to reach 470,000 people; of which 167,000 are children**. UNICEF’s earthquake response and is fully aligned with the addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) in Venezuela, which targets **1.3 million people affected by the earthquake** across 7 states. passages.title: One month after earthquakes, Venezuela risks spiraling into deeper crisis without urgent investment in economic recovery
passages.text: Caracas, Venezuela, July 22, 2026 — Nearly one month after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, the window is closing to set the country on a sustainable path toward recovery. Without immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support, the disaster risks spiraling into a deeper humanitarian crisis, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns. Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty]( Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins. Now, the economic situation threatens to unravel further. An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes.

July 2026 Following the June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela, Project HOPE and its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a needs assessment across 12 health facilities and 160 households in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira to evaluate health service capacity, WASH conditions, and community protection needs. The assessment found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support services, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure, and protection mechanisms, despite generally strong community knowledge of disease prevention and existing health system capacity. Findings indicate that humanitarian response efforts should prioritize restoring essential health supplies and infrastructure, strengthening WASH systems, expanding mental health and protection services, and addressing barriers that prevent communities and health facilities from translating existing knowledge into effective practices. passages.text: Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June 2026. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas. The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents. The health system is under severe strain. Many health facilities have sustained structural damage and are facing critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and personnel, while disruptions to electricity, water supply and supply chains continue to hamper service delivery. To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas. UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information.

passages.title: Situation Report No.9: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 August 2026
passages.text: **HIGHLIGHTS** Seven weeks after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response continues to sustain emergency operations while transitioning toward early recovery. Current efforts are focused on maintaining essential health services, rehabilitating affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and delivering health services through a comprehensive approach, while mitigating public health risks and ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment. Health service recovery and critical care capacity are advancing, with rehabilitation planning progressing in priority facilities and intensive care and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, while assessments in Caracas and Miranda continue to identify critical gaps in equipment and human resources. Public health surveillance and immunization systems are being reinforced, with expanded epidemiological analysis and digital reporting, enhanced laboratory diagnostic capacity, and more than 31,000 vaccine doses administered; national vaccine supply security was further supported through a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line. Efforts advanced toward the provision of comprehensive care, focusing on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, noncommunicable diseases, and rehabilitation. This included dissemination of the national mental health protocol, training of transitional camp focal points, continuity of oncology care through three designated centers, and attention to emerging needs such as assessing rehabilitation center capacities and training on amputee management and wound care. PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, most recently delivering targeted emergency medical supplies – including specialized kits, medicines, and high-complexity surgical instruments – to the Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere in Petare, Sucre.
